question: A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes is on insulin with an HbA1c of 52 mmol/mol. His urine ACR is 4.2 mg/mmol on two separate occasions 3 months apart. His BP is 138/86 mmHg. Per NICE NG28, what medication should be added to slow diabetic nephropathy progression?

options.A: Increase insulin dose only — HbA1c is the priority
options.B: Lisinopril (ACE inhibitor) — first-line for diabetic nephropathy with microalbuminuria regardless of blood pressure; reduces intraglomerular pressure and urinary albumin excretion, slowing CKD progression
options.C: Amlodipine — calcium channel blockers are first-line for renal protection in diabetes
options.D: Bendroflumethiazide — diuretics are the best choice in diabetic kidney disease
options.E: No additional medication — ACR 4.2 mg/mmol is within normal limits

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG28 (Type 2 diabetes in adults), ACE inhibitors or ARBs are the treatment of choice for diabetic nephropathy. An ACR of 3-30 mg/mmol represents microalbuminuria (A2 category per NICE NG203). In a diabetic patient with microalbuminuria, an ACE inhibitor (lisinopril, ramipril) or ARB (losartan, candesartan) should be started regardless of blood pressure — they provide specific renoprotective effects by reducing intraglomerular hypertension and albuminuria beyond just blood pressure lowering. Target BP in diabetes with CKD: <130/80 mmHg. An SGLT2 inhibitor (dapagliflozin) should also be considered per NICE NG28/NG203 to reduce CKD progression.
explanation.A: Incorrect — HbA1c 52 mmol/mol is at target; the microalbuminuria requires specific renoprotection with an ACE inhibitor.
explanation.B: CORRECT — ACE inhibitor (lisinopril) is first-line for diabetic nephropathy with microalbuminuria per NICE NG28 regardless of BP.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Calcium channel blockers lower blood pressure but do not provide specific renoprotection against diabetic nephropathy.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Thiazide diuretics are not first-line for renal protection in diabetic nephropathy.
explanation.E: Incorrect — ACR 4.2 mg/mmol is in the A2 (microalbuminuria) category per NICE NG203 (A2 = 3-30 mg/mmol) — action is required.

reference: NICE NG28 — Type 2 diabetes in adults. NICE NG203 — CKD. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng28

question: A 52-year-old man with type 1 diabetes on insulin has a urine ACR of 38 mg/mmol and eGFR 55 ml/min. He is already on ramipril 10mg. His BP is 126/78 mmHg. His HbA1c is 68 mmol/mol. Per current NICE guidance, what additional intervention would reduce his renal risk?

options.A: Add an ARB alongside the ACE inhibitor — dual blockade is recommended
options.B: Optimise glycaemic control — reducing HbA1c to below 53 mmol/mol using more intensive insulin management is the most evidence-based additional intervention for reducing diabetic nephropathy progression alongside ACE inhibitor therapy
options.C: Add spironolactone for additional renal protection
options.E: Dual ACE inhibitor and ARB therapy provides superior renal protection

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG17 (Type 1 diabetes in adults) and NICE NG203, in type 1 diabetes with established diabetic nephropathy, the two pillars of renoprotection are: (1) Glycaemic optimisation — every 1% (11 mmol/mol) reduction in HbA1c significantly reduces microvascular complications including nephropathy (DCCT trial); target HbA1c ≤53 mmol/mol where achievable; (2) ACE inhibitor/ARB (already prescribed). Dual ACE inhibitor + ARB blockade (e.g., ramipril + losartan) was previously studied but ONTARGET trial showed increased adverse effects (hyperkalaemia, AKI, acute renal failure) without mortality benefit — this combination is NOT recommended. SGLT2 inhibitors have emerging evidence in type 1 diabetes but are not currently NICE-approved for T1DM renal indication.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Dual renin-angiotensin blockade (ACE + ARB) is not recommended per ONTARGET trial — increased adverse effects without mortality benefit.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Optimising glycaemic control (reduce HbA1c towards 53 mmol/mol) is the key additional intervention for diabetic nephropathy per NICE NG17.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Spironolactone in CKD with ACE inhibitor risks dangerous hyperkalaemia — not recommended.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Doubling ramipril beyond 10mg is not a licensed strategy for additional renoprotection.
explanation.E: Incorrect — ACE + ARB dual blockade is specifically NOT recommended per ONTARGET — avoid.

reference: NICE NG17 — Type 1 diabetes. DCCT trial. ONTARGET trial. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng17

question: A GP is conducting an annual diabetic foot review. Per NICE NG19 and the diabetic foot pathway, which assessment tool is used for diabetic peripheral neuropathy screening in primary care?

options.B: 10-gram monofilament test — pressure applied to 3-4 standard sites on the plantar surface of the foot; inability to feel the monofilament indicates loss of protective sensation and high risk of foot ulceration
options.E: Nerve conduction studies at each annual review

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG19 (Diabetic foot problems: prevention and management) and NICE NG28, annual diabetic foot assessment in primary care includes: (1) 10-gram monofilament test — a calibrated Semmes-Weinstein 10g monofilament is applied to 3-4 sites on the plantar foot (excluding any callus); inability to feel the monofilament = loss of protective sensation = high risk of ulceration. This is the gold standard neuropathy screening tool in primary care; (2) Vibration sensation (128 Hz tuning fork); (3) Pedal pulses + ABPI for vascular assessment; (4) Inspection for deformity, callus, ulceration, skin condition. A 23-gauge needle is NOT appropriate — it can cause injury and is not the validated screening tool for protective sensation.
explanation.A: Incorrect — A 23-gauge needle carries risk of injury and is not the validated tool for diabetic neuropathy screening. The 10g monofilament is the correct instrument.
explanation.B: CORRECT — 10-gram monofilament is the validated primary care screening tool for diabetic peripheral neuropathy per NICE NG19.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Tuning fork (128 Hz) tests vibration sensation — it is part of the assessment but not the primary neuropathy screening tool.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Visual inspection alone misses sensory neuropathy which is the key ulceration risk factor.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Nerve conduction studies are specialist investigations — not appropriate for routine annual primary care diabetic foot review.

reference: NICE NG19 — Diabetic foot problems. NICE NG28 — Type 2 diabetes. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng19

question: A 42-year-old woman presents with fatigue, weight loss, muscle weakness, postural dizziness and increased skin pigmentation. Blood tests show sodium 128 mmol/L, potassium 5.8 mmol/L, and raised ACTH. Per NICE CKS, what is the most likely diagnosis and first-line investigation to confirm it?

options.B: Addison's disease (primary adrenal insufficiency) — confirmed by a short Synacthen test (SST): 250 mcg tetracosactide IV/IM; cortisol measured at 0 and 30 minutes; a peak cortisol <450 nmol/L (or <500 in some labs) at 30 minutes confirms adrenal insufficiency
options.C: Hypothyroidism — TSH is the confirmatory test

explanation.correct: Addison's disease (primary adrenal insufficiency): autoimmune destruction of the adrenal cortex is the most common cause in the UK (70-80%). Classic features: fatigue, weight loss, anorexia, nausea, postural hypotension, muscle weakness, salt craving, skin and mucous membrane hyperpigmentation (due to excess ACTH stimulating melanocytes). Biochemistry: hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, raised ACTH (high because the failing adrenals don't produce cortisol to feedback negatively), low cortisol. Per NICE CKS: confirmatory test is the short Synacthen test (SST) — 250 mcg tetracosactide IV; cortisol measured at 0 and 30 minutes. Peak cortisol <450 nmol/L = inadequate response = adrenal insufficiency. Emergency management if adrenal crisis: IV hydrocortisone 100mg immediately.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Cushing's syndrome causes HYPERTENSION, weight gain, moon face, purple striae — not hypotension, hyperkalaemia and hyperpigmentation.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Addison's disease: confirmed by short Synacthen test. Peak cortisol <450 nmol/L at 30 minutes per NICE CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Hypothyroidism causes weight gain, cold intolerance, constipation — not hyperkalaemia and skin pigmentation.
explanation.D: Incorrect — SIADH causes hyponatraemia but NOT hyperkalaemia or skin pigmentation.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Conn's syndrome (primary hyperaldosteronism) causes HYPERTENSION + hypokalaemia — the opposite electrolyte picture to Addison's.

question: A 38-year-old woman with known Addison's disease on hydrocortisone 10mg/10mg/5mg and fludrocortisone 100 mcg daily develops vomiting and diarrhoea from gastroenteritis. She cannot keep her oral medications down. Per NICE CKS and patient sick day rules, what must she do?

options.A: Skip hydrocortisone until vomiting settles — steroids worsen gastroenteritis
options.B: Administer hydrocortisone 100mg IM (emergency injection kit) immediately — vomiting preventing oral absorption of steroids in an Addison's patient is a life-threatening adrenal crisis. Every patient with Addison's disease should have an emergency injection kit and be trained to use it (or have a family member trained); call 999 and go to hospital for IV hydrocortisone
options.C: Double the oral dose and try to keep it down
options.D: Take fludrocortisone only — more important than hydrocortisone during illness
options.E: Wait 24 hours before acting — minor illness does not require action

explanation.correct: Adrenal crisis (Addisonian crisis) is a life-threatening emergency caused by acute cortisol deficiency — most commonly triggered by illness (infection, vomiting, diarrhoea), surgery or injury in patients with Addison's disease who cannot absorb or take their replacement steroids. Sick day rules per NICE CKS and Addison's Disease Self Help Group (ADSHG): (1) Mild illness (fever, vomiting once): double or triple oral hydrocortisone dose; (2) Unable to keep oral medication down: administer 100mg IM hydrocortisone from emergency injection kit immediately; (3) Call 999 and go to A&E for IV hydrocortisone infusion and fluids. Every Addison's patient must: carry an emergency injection kit (hydrocortisone 100mg powder for injection + diluent), wear a medical alert bracelet, carry a steroid emergency card, and receive education on sick day rules. Failure to act leads to circulatory collapse and death.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Withholding steroids during illness in an Addison's patient causes adrenal crisis — this is immediately life-threatening.
explanation.B: CORRECT — IM hydrocortisone 100mg from emergency kit immediately + 999 for IV steroids per NICE CKS / ADSHG sick day rules.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Doubling oral dose during vomiting is insufficient — oral absorption is unreliable when vomiting. IM injection is required.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Fludrocortisone replaces mineralocorticoid (aldosterone) — it is the hydrocortisone (glucocorticoid) that is life-saving in an acute crisis.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Waiting 24 hours in a vomiting Addison's patient who cannot absorb oral steroids risks fatal adrenal crisis.

reference: NICE CKS — Addison's disease: sick day rules. ADSHG — Emergency injection. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/addisons-disease/

question: A 35-year-old woman with Addison's disease is due to have an elective dental extraction under local anaesthesia. Per NICE CKS and endocrine society guidance on perioperative steroid management, what advice should be given?

options.A: No change to steroids — dental procedures do not require dose adjustment
options.B: For minor procedures under local anaesthesia: take usual morning hydrocortisone dose; for moderate procedures: double the dose on the day; for major surgery under general anaesthesia: IV hydrocortisone is required — inform the surgical and anaesthetic team
options.C: Stop hydrocortisone 48 hours before the procedure to prevent infection
options.D: Quadruple the dose for 1 week before and after any dental procedure
options.E: Switch to prednisolone for 2 weeks perioperatively

explanation.correct: Per NICE CKS and Society for Endocrinology perioperative guidelines, patients with Addison's disease require supplemental steroids (sick day rules) during surgical stress as their adrenals cannot mount an appropriate cortisol stress response. Dental procedures under local anaesthesia: take normal morning hydrocortisone dose — no additional supplementation usually needed for very minor procedures. Moderate procedures (minor surgery, GA): double or triple the hydrocortisone dose on the day (e.g., usual 10mg → 20-30mg morning of procedure). Major surgery under GA: IV hydrocortisone 100mg at induction, then 200-300mg/24 hours by infusion, tapered to usual dose when eating and drinking. Always inform the surgical team that the patient has Addison's disease — anaesthetic and surgical team must know. Patient should carry steroid emergency card.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Dental extraction is a stressful procedure — Addison's patients may need dose adjustment depending on the extent of procedure and anaesthesia used.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Stratified perioperative steroid supplementation based on procedure severity per NICE CKS / Society for Endocrinology guidelines.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Stopping steroids perioperatively in an Addison's patient causes adrenal crisis — this is dangerous and incorrect.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Quadrupling steroids for a week is excessive and unnecessary for minor dental procedures.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Switching to prednisolone unnecessarily changes the patient's established regimen; dose adjustment of hydrocortisone is the appropriate approach.

reference: Society for Endocrinology — Perioperative steroid management. NICE CKS — Addison's disease. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/addisons-disease/

question: A 48-year-old woman presents with hypertension resistant to three antihypertensives, weight gain, central obesity, thin skin, purple striae and proximal muscle weakness. Per NICE CKS, what is the most appropriate first-line screening test for Cushing's syndrome?

options.B: Overnight dexamethasone suppression test (ONDST) — 1mg dexamethasone taken at 11pm; cortisol measured at 8-9am the next morning; cortisol >50 nmol/L = failure to suppress = screen positive for Cushing's syndrome

explanation.correct: Per NICE CKS (Cushing's syndrome) and the Endocrine Society guidelines, three first-line screening tests are acceptable: (1) Overnight dexamethasone suppression test (ONDST) — 1mg dexamethasone at 11pm, cortisol at 8-9am next morning; >50 nmol/L = positive; (2) 24-hour urinary free cortisol (UFC) — at least two measurements; (3) Late-night salivary cortisol — less commonly used in UK primary care. The ONDST is the most practical for primary care — simple, outpatient, high sensitivity (~95%). A positive screening test should be followed by confirmatory testing (LDDST, 24-hour UFC) and referral to endocrinology. Note: exogenous steroid use (including topical, inhaled, injected) can cause iatrogenic Cushing's — exclude this first. A random cortisol is not useful (wide diurnal variation).
explanation.A: Incorrect — Random serum cortisol has too much variation throughout the day to be a useful screening test for Cushing's syndrome.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Overnight dexamethasone suppression test (1mg at 11pm; cortisol >50 nmol/L = positive) is first-line screening per NICE CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — ACTH level differentiates ACTH-dependent (Cushing's disease, ectopic) from ACTH-independent causes but cannot screen for Cushing's syndrome.
explanation.D: Incorrect — MRI pituitary is performed after biochemical confirmation of Cushing's disease (ACTH-dependent) — not first-line screening.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Short Synacthen test diagnoses adrenal insufficiency (Addison's) — the opposite condition to Cushing's.

reference: NICE CKS — Cushing's syndrome. Endocrine Society — Cushing's Syndrome Guidelines. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/cushings-syndrome/

question: A 52-year-old man has biochemically confirmed Cushing's syndrome (elevated 24-hour urinary cortisol, failed overnight DST). His ACTH is suppressed at <1 pmol/L. Per NICE CKS and endocrinological guidelines, what does suppressed ACTH indicate and what is the next investigation?

options.A: Suppressed ACTH indicates pituitary adenoma (Cushing's disease)
options.B: Suppressed ACTH indicates ACTH-independent Cushing's syndrome — the adrenal gland is autonomously producing cortisol (independently of ACTH). Next investigation: adrenal CT or MRI to identify adrenal adenoma, carcinoma or bilateral adrenal hyperplasia
options.C: Suppressed ACTH indicates ectopic ACTH secretion
options.D: Suppressed ACTH is a normal finding in Cushing's syndrome — no further investigation needed
options.E: Suppressed ACTH confirms hypothalamic dysfunction — MRI brain required

explanation.correct: ACTH measurement is the critical investigation to differentiate Cushing's syndrome subtypes: ACTH suppressed (<1-2 pmol/L) = ACTH-independent (adrenal source): cortisol is being produced autonomously by the adrenal gland; high cortisol feeds back to suppress pituitary ACTH. Causes: adrenal adenoma (most common unilateral), adrenal carcinoma, bilateral adrenal hyperplasia. Next step: adrenal CT/MRI. ACTH elevated or normal = ACTH-dependent: pituitary adenoma (Cushing's disease — most common overall, ~70%) or ectopic ACTH secretion (e.g., small cell lung carcinoma). For ACTH-dependent: high-dose DST ± inferior petrosal sinus sampling to distinguish pituitary vs ectopic source. Adrenal adenoma causing Cushing's: treated by laparoscopic adrenalectomy.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Pituitary adenoma (Cushing's disease) causes ELEVATED ACTH — not suppressed.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Suppressed ACTH = ACTH-independent Cushing's from adrenal source. Adrenal CT/MRI is next per NICE CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Ectopic ACTH secretion causes very HIGH ACTH — not suppressed.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Suppressed ACTH is a clinically significant finding directing the investigation pathway to adrenal imaging.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Hypothalamic dysfunction is not the interpretation of a suppressed ACTH in confirmed Cushing's syndrome.

reference: NICE CKS — Cushing's syndrome. Endocrine Society Guidelines. https://cks.nice.org.uk/topics/cushings-syndrome/

question: A 55-year-old man with hypertension has features of Cushing's syndrome. His GP first considers iatrogenic Cushing's. Per NICE CKS, which medication history is most important to take before requesting biochemical tests?

options.A: ACE inhibitor history — ramipril causes Cushingoid features
options.B: Exogenous corticosteroid use — any route (oral, inhaled, topical, intra-articular, epidural, nasal) can cause iatrogenic Cushing's syndrome and will invalidate biochemical screening tests; this must be excluded before formal testing
options.D: Alcohol history — alcohol causes pseudo-Cushing's, biochemically similar but clinically different
options.E: Statin use — associated with cortisol metabolism changes

explanation.correct: Per NICE CKS, the most common cause of Cushing's syndrome globally is iatrogenic — exogenous corticosteroid use by ANY route. Before biochemical testing for endogenous Cushing's, a thorough corticosteroid history must be taken including: oral prednisolone/dexamethasone; high-dose inhaled corticosteroids (e.g., fluticasone, budesonide); potent topical steroids (clobetasol); intra-articular, epidural, or intramuscular corticosteroid injections; nasal corticosteroids (smaller risk). Exogenous corticosteroids: suppress ACTH and endogenous cortisol; cause a positive dexamethasone suppression test (no endogenous cortisol to suppress); mimic Cushing's syndrome biochemically. Alcohol use causes pseudo-Cushing's (positive biochemical tests) — also important to exclude but iatrogenic steroids are more common.
explanation.A: Incorrect — ACE inhibitors do not cause Cushingoid features or interfere with cortisol testing.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Exogenous corticosteroid use by any route must be excluded before biochemical Cushing's testing — it causes iatrogenic Cushing's per NICE CKS.
explanation.C: Incorrect — NSAIDs do not cause cortisol elevation or Cushingoid features.
explanation.D: Incorrect — Alcohol causes pseudo-Cushing's (important to exclude) but the most important medication history is corticosteroid use.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Statins do not cause Cushingoid features or cortisol metabolism changes of clinical significance.

question: A 52-year-old man is newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes. His HbA1c is 62 mmol/mol and his BMI is 32 kg/m². He has no CKD or cardiovascular disease. Per NICE NG28, what is the first-line pharmacological treatment?

options.A: Gliclazide — most effective for rapid HbA1c reduction
options.B: Metformin — first-line for all newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes regardless of BMI, providing no contraindication (eGFR ≥30, no hepatic impairment); start at 500mg daily with food, titrate to 1g twice daily over 4 weeks to reduce GI side effects
options.C: Insulin — required for HbA1c >58 mmol/mol at diagnosis
options.D: Sitagliptin (DPP-4 inhibitor) — preferred for overweight patients
options.E: Empagliflozin alone — most effective for BMI 32

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG28, metformin is the first-line pharmacological treatment for type 2 diabetes regardless of BMI, unless contraindicated. Contraindications: eGFR <30 ml/min (absolute), eGFR 30-45 (use with caution, reduce dose), hepatic impairment, acute illness with dehydration. Starting regime: standard-release metformin 500mg once or twice daily with meals, increase by 500mg every 1-2 weeks to target dose of 2g/day (or maximum tolerated); modified-release formulation if GI intolerance. If HbA1c remains above target (>53 mmol/mol) at 3-6 months: add a second agent (SGLT2 inhibitor if CVD/CKD/HF; DPP-4 inhibitor or sulfonylurea otherwise). NICE NG28 also recommends SGLT2 inhibitor earlier if the patient has established CVD or high CV risk.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Gliclazide (sulfonylurea) is second or third-line in NICE NG28 — metformin is first-line.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Metformin first-line for T2DM regardless of BMI per NICE NG28. Start low, titrate slowly to reduce GI side effects.
explanation.C: Incorrect — Insulin is not first-line for newly diagnosed T2DM — dietary intervention and metformin should be tried first unless HbA1c is very high (>86 mmol/mol) or symptomatic hyperglycaemia.
explanation.D: Incorrect — DPP-4 inhibitors are second-line add-on therapy per NICE NG28 — not first-line.
explanation.E: Incorrect — SGLT2 inhibitors (empagliflozin) are indicated as first-line alongside metformin in high cardiovascular risk T2DM but not as monotherapy first-line at this HbA1c.

reference: NICE NG28 — Type 2 diabetes in adults: management. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng28

question: A patient with type 1 diabetes on a basal-bolus insulin regime has blood glucose readings: fasting morning BG consistently 9-11 mmol/L, post-meal lunch BG 12-14 mmol/L, and post-meal dinner BG 10-12 mmol/L. All other readings are above target. Per NICE NG17 and insulin adjustment principles, which insulin should be adjusted first?

options.A: Increase all meal-time (bolus) insulin doses equally
options.B: Increase the basal (background) insulin dose — consistently elevated fasting morning glucose across the day indicates insufficient basal insulin; once fasting is at target (4-7 mmol/L), reassess post-meal readings before adjusting bolus doses
options.C: Start a GLP-1 receptor agonist to reduce all readings
options.D: Reduce carbohydrate intake only — no insulin change needed
options.E: Switch to premixed insulin — simplifies the regime

explanation.correct: Per NICE NG17 and DAFNE (Dose Adjustment For Normal Eating) principles, structured insulin adjustment in type 1 diabetes follows this logic: Consistently elevated fasting/morning glucose → increase BASAL insulin first. Once fasting glucose is at target (4-7 mmol/L): reassess post-meal readings. Elevated post-meal readings with normal fasting → increase the corresponding BOLUS (meal-time) dose. Rationale: if fasting glucose is high, the background insulin is insufficient regardless of meal insulin; adjusting bolus doses on top of insufficient basal leads to compounding errors. NICE NG17: structured education (DAFNE for type 1, DESMOND for type 2) teaches patients to adjust their own insulin. Basal adjustment: typically increase by 2 units every 3 days until fasting within target.
explanation.A: Incorrect — Increasing all bolus doses equally when fasting glucose is elevated risks post-meal hypoglycaemia while the root problem (insufficient basal) is unaddressed.
explanation.B: CORRECT — Elevated fasting BG = insufficient basal insulin. Increase basal first, then reassess bolus needs per NICE NG17/DAFNE principles.
explanation.C: Incorrect — GLP-1 agonists are not licensed for type 1 diabetes in standard UK practice.
explanation.D: Incorrect — While dietary management is important, the pattern of consistently elevated readings indicates insulin underdosing that must be corrected.
explanation.E: Incorrect — Switching to premixed insulin removes the flexibility of independent basal/bolus adjustment — not appropriate for consistently elevated all-day readings in type 1 diabetes.

reference: NICE NG17 — Type 1 diabetes in adults. DAFNE programme. https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng17
